steps.body:
A solid does not have to be made by revolving anything. Stand a **square** on every slice of a flat region and you get a solid just as real — and just as easy.

The slice's area is whatever the cross-section's area is. If the side is s = f(x), a square slice is **s²**, and

**V = ∫ₐᵇ [f(x)]² dx.**

And notice: **no π anywhere.** π only appeared because a disc is a circle.
The disc mode, one last time — and then let go of the circle.

widget.prompt: Revolve y = x on [0, 2] and each slice is a circle of area πr². Get the sum within 0.05 of 8π/3 — then ask what would change if the slice were a SQUARE instead.
widget.successFeedback: 8π/3, from circular slices. Now change one thing in your head: make each slice a SQUARE of side r instead of a circle of radius r. Its area is r² rather than πr² — so the whole volume loses its π and becomes ∫₀² x² dx = 8/3. Same slicing, same summing. Only the shape standing on the slice has changed.
widget.lowFeedback: The stack is under 8π/3. Raise the count, or try the midpoint rule.
widget.highFeedback: The stack is over 8π/3. Raise the count and it will settle.

cml.actionGoal: Refine cross-sectional slices and connect their accumulated volume estimate to a limiting integral.

predict.prompt: Keep every slice's size the same but make each cross-section a SQUARE of side r instead of a circle of radius r. The total volume will be…

options.label: Bigger — a square has corners the circle lacks
The same — the slices are the same size

predict.reveal: Smaller. A square of side r has area r², while the circle of radius r has πr² ≈ 3.14 r² — the circle is inscribed in a square of side 2r, not r. Notice what had to change to answer that: one formula. Slice, find ONE cross-section's area, integrate. The circle was never load-bearing.

explanationVariants: A square of side x has area x², so V = ∫₀² x² dx = 8/3 ≈ 2.667. The π has vanished, because nothing here is round.
The circle contributed the π. Take the circle away and the π goes with it.

widget.prompt: The base is the region under y = x on [0, 2]. Cross-sections perpendicular to the x-axis are SQUARES with side y = x. Find the volume, to three decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 8π/3 — the answer for CIRCULAR slices. A square of side x has area x², not πx², so the π disappears entirely.
That is the length of the base interval. The volume is ∫₀² x² dx = 8/3.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Square slices have area x², so V = ∫₀² x² dx = 8/3 ≈ 2.667 — no π, because nothing is round.

explanationVariants: An equilateral triangle of side s has area (√3/4)s². So V = (√3/4)∫₀² x² dx = (√3/4)(8/3) ≈ 1.155.
The constant out front is whatever the shape's area formula gives. The integral ∫s² dx never changes.

widget.prompt: The slices are equilateral TRIANGLES of side s = f(x), instead of squares. What changes?

options.label: Only the constant: multiply the same ∫[f(x)]² dx by √3/4, the triangle's area coefficient.
options.feedback: Right. The slicing and the summing are untouched — only the shape's area formula changes, and it contributes a constant out front.

options.label: You must revolve the region first.
options.feedback: Nothing is being revolved here at all. The triangles are simply STANDING on the base, like fins.

options.label: The integral becomes ∫f(x) dx.
options.feedback: A triangle's area still depends on the side SQUARED, so the integrand keeps its [f(x)]².

options.label: You cannot integrate triangular slices.
options.feedback: You can integrate ANY slice whose area you can write down. That is the whole liberation of this method.

steps.body:
So the recipe is completely general:

**Work out the area of ONE cross-section, in terms of x.** Then integrate it.

Square → s². Equilateral triangle → (√3/4)s². Semicircle → (π/8)s². Circle → πr².

The calculus never notices which. It only ever adds up slices — and the geometry of the slice is your job, not the integral's.

explanationVariants: A semicircle of DIAMETER s has radius s/2, so its area is (1/2)π(s/2)² = (π/8)s². Then V = (π/8)(8/3) = π/3 ≈ 1.047.
The trap is using s as the radius instead of the diameter — that would give four times too much.

widget.prompt: Same base (under y = x on [0, 2]), but the slices are SEMICIRCLES of diameter s = x. Find the volume, to three decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That treats x as the RADIUS. It is the DIAMETER, so the radius is x/2 and the area is (π/8)x², not (π/2)x².
That is the answer for SQUARE slices. A semicircle of diameter x has area (π/8)x², so the volume is (π/8)(8/3) = π/3.
That is a full circle of radius x — twice too round and twice too big. Halve it, and remember x is the diameter.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Semicircle of diameter x: area (π/8)x², so V = (π/8)(8/3) = π/3 ≈ 1.047.

hints: The area of an equilateral triangle with side s is (√3/4)s². Here s = x.
So the integral is (√3/4)∫₀² x² dx.
explanationVariants: Every one of these problems is the same two steps: write down the area of ONE slice, then integrate it. The difficulty is never the calculus.

widget.prompt: Base under y = x on [0, 2], with equilateral-TRIANGLE cross-sections of side x. Find the volume, to three decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the SQUARE answer, ∫x² = 8/3. A triangle of side s has area (√3/4)s², so multiply by √3/4 ≈ 0.433.
That is half of the answer — perhaps you used (√3/8). The equilateral triangle's coefficient is √3/4.
That looks like a factor of 4 out. (√3/4)(8/3) ≈ 1.155.

steps.body: Any slice you can measure, you can integrate.
takeaways: No revolution is needed. Stand ANY shape on the slices and the method is unchanged.
Write the area of ONE cross-section in terms of x, then integrate it. That is the whole method.
π appears only when the slice is round. Square slices have no π — which is a useful sanity check.
steps.teaser: Next: the one number that could stand in for a whole function.

concept.body: What shape is standing on the slice, and what is its AREA? Write that in terms of x, then integrate it. The calculus does not care whether the shape is a circle, a square or a triangle — only you do.

explanationVariants: A square of side 3 has area 9. No π, because a square is not round.

widget.prompt: A square cross-section has side 3. What is its area?

commonErrors.feedback: That is π(3²) — the area of a CIRCLE of radius 3. A square of side 3 has area 9, with no π at all.
That is the PERIMETER, 4 × 3. The area is 3² = 9.
